# The blanket conjecture is FALSE (boundary of the instability theorem)

The research mission's headline claim is

> "For any Cayley digraph `G` of an abelian group of even order, the pair
> `(G, K₂)` is unstable."

This file **refutes** that blanket claim with an explicit, machine-checked
counterexample, and thereby pins down the exact boundary of the positive
results in `Instability.lean`.

## Main result

* `cay_Z4_01_stable` — every automorphism of the double cover of
  `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is of the expected form; equivalently `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is
  **stable**.
* `blanket_conjecture_false` — consequently there *is* an even-order abelian
  Cayley digraph that is not unstable, so the blanket conjecture fails.

`Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is connected (the generator `1` already connects all of `ℤ₄`)
and non-bipartite (the loop `0 ∈ S` gives odd closed walks), so the
counterexample is not a degenerate "disconnected/bipartite" artefact.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Experiment (Stage 2): exhaustive computation over all `S ⊆ ℤ₄` (see
`ComputationalEvidence.md`) found `|Aut(BX)| = 2·|Aut(X)|` exactly for
`S ∈ {{0,1},{0,3},{1,2},{2,3},{1,2,3}}`.  The smallest is `S = {0,1}`.

Analysis (Stage 3): classification of even-order circulants.
  * `χ(S)` constant (`S` in the even subgroup, or `S` entirely odd) ⇒ unstable
    — this is the *true* core, proved constructively in `Instability.lean`.
  * `χ(S)` mixed ⇒ instability is genuinely *not* automatic; `{0,1}` is stable
    while `{0,1,2}` is unstable.  So the blanket claim is FALSE, and parity of
    the connection set alone does not decide stability.

Critique (Stage 4): the witness here uses `native_decide` (a finite search over
the 40320 permutations of the 8-vertex double cover).  It is deliberately a
*secondary* result; the main theorems of this development are the constructive,
search-free instability theorems in `Instability.lean`.  The finite check is
the most honest certificate of a *negative* (universally quantified over all
automorphisms) statement.
-/
import Mathlib
import Applications.CayleyDoubleCover.Core

namespace CayleyDoubleCover.Boundary

open CayleyDoubleCover

/-- The connection set `{0, 1}` of the circulant on `ℤ₄`. -/
def S01 : Finset (ZMod 4) := {0, 1}

instance : DecidablePred (IsDCAut S01) := fun e => by unfold IsDCAut; infer_instance
instance : DecidablePred (IsExpected (A := ZMod 4)) := fun e => by
  unfold IsExpected; infer_instance

/-- **Stability of `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})`.**
Every automorphism of its canonical double cover has the expected form
`(a,i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)`.  Verified by exhaustive search over the symmetric group
on the 8 vertices of the double cover. -/
theorem cay_Z4_01_stable :
    ∀ e : Equiv.Perm (ZMod 4 × Bool), IsDCAut S01 e → IsExpected e := by
  native_decide

/-- `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is **not** unstable. -/
theorem not_unstable_S01 : ¬ Unstable S01 := by
  rintro ⟨e, hAut, hExp⟩
  exact hExp (cay_Z4_01_stable e hAut)

/-- **The blanket conjecture is false.**
There is an even-order abelian Cayley digraph whose pair with `K₂` is *stable*:
`ℤ₄` has even order, `2 ∣ 4`, yet `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is not unstable. -/
theorem blanket_conjecture_false :
    ∃ (n : ℕ), (2 ∣ n) ∧ ∃ (S : Finset (ZMod n)), ¬ Unstable S :=
  ⟨4, by norm_num, S01, not_unstable_S01⟩

end CayleyDoubleCover.Boundary

# Stability of Cayley Digraphs and their Canonical Double Cover (Core definitions)

This file sets up a self-contained, *computable* framework for studying the
**stability** of a Cayley digraph `Cay(A, S)` of a (finite) abelian group `A`
under the canonical double cover operation `· × K₂`.

## The objects

* Vertices of `Cay(A, S)` are the elements of `A`; there is an arc `a → b`
  iff `b - a ∈ S`.
* The **canonical double cover** (a.k.a. tensor product with `K₂`,
  the "bipartite double") has vertex set `A × Bool`, with an arc
  `p → q` iff `p.2 ≠ q.2` (we cross the two layers) and `q.1 - p.1 ∈ S`.
  This is `DCadj`.
* An **automorphism** of the double cover is a permutation of `A × Bool`
  preserving `DCadj` (`IsDCAut`).
* Every double cover automatically carries the "expected" automorphisms
  `(a, i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)` coming from `Aut(Cay(A,S)) × ℤ₂` (`IsExpected`).
* `Cay(A, S)` is **unstable** when there is an automorphism of its double
  cover that is *not* of the expected form (`Unstable`).  This is exactly the
  statement `Aut(Cay(A,S) × K₂) ≠ Aut(Cay(A,S)) × ℤ₂`.

All predicates are kept `Decidable` (no `Classical`) so that concrete instances
can be settled by `decide` / `native_decide` in `Boundary.lean`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Stage 1): "(G, K₂) is unstable for every Cayley digraph G of an
abelian group of even order."  To even *state* this we need a faithful, finite,
decidable model of the double cover and of the splitting `Aut(X) × ℤ₂`.

Experiment (Stage 2): we modelled the double cover on `A × Bool` with the
single uniform arc rule `p.2 ≠ q.2 ∧ q.1 - p.1 ∈ S` (valid for *digraphs*,
not just graphs — we do **not** assume `S = -S`).  A short brute force over
`ℤ₄, ℤ₆` (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`) confirmed the model reproduces the
known automorphism counts, e.g. `|Aut(Cay(ℤ₄,{1}) × K₂)| = 32`.

Analysis (Stage 3): the *expected* subgroup is precisely the image of the
homomorphism `Aut(X) × ℤ₂ → Aut(X × K₂)`, whose elements have the rigid shape
`(a,i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)`; instability ⇔ this map is not surjective.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace CayleyDoubleCover

variable {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A]

/-- Adjacency of the canonical double cover of `Cay(A, S)`:
there is an arc `p → q` iff the two `Bool`-layers differ and `q.1 - p.1 ∈ S`. -/
def DCadj (S : Finset A) (p q : A × Bool) : Prop :=
  p.2 ≠ q.2 ∧ (q.1 - p.1 ∈ S)

instance (S : Finset A) [DecidableEq A] : DecidableRel (DCadj S) := fun p q => by
  unfold DCadj; infer_instance

/-- A double-cover automorphism: a permutation of `A × Bool` preserving `DCadj`. -/
def IsDCAut (S : Finset A) (e : Equiv.Perm (A × Bool)) : Prop :=
  ∀ p q, DCadj S (e p) (e q) ↔ DCadj S p q

/-- The "expected" automorphisms coming from `Aut(Cay(A,S)) × ℤ₂`:
those of the form `(a, i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)` for a fixed permutation `σ` of `A`
and a fixed `ε : Bool` (the deck transformation flag). -/
def IsExpected (e : Equiv.Perm (A × Bool)) : Prop :=
  ∃ (σ : Equiv.Perm A) (ε : Bool), ∀ p : A × Bool, e p = (σ p.1, xor p.2 ε)

/-- `Cay(A, S)` is **unstable** iff its canonical double cover has an
automorphism that is not of the expected form. -/
def Unstable (S : Finset A) : Prop :=
  ∃ e, IsDCAut S e ∧ ¬ IsExpected e

/-- The candidate "unexpected" automorphism attached to a parity character
`χ : A → Bool`: it fixes the first coordinate and flips the layer of `(a,i)`
exactly when `χ a = true`.  It is always an involution, hence a permutation. -/
def chiSwap (χ : A → Bool) : Equiv.Perm (A × Bool) where
  toFun p := (p.1, xor p.2 (χ p.1))
  invFun p := (p.1, xor p.2 (χ p.1))
  left_inv p := by simp
  right_inv p := by simp

omit [AddCommGroup A] in
@[simp] lemma chiSwap_apply (χ : A → Bool) (p : A × Bool) :
    chiSwap χ p = (p.1, xor p.2 (χ p.1)) := rfl

end CayleyDoubleCover

# Instability of Cayley digraphs via a parity character (Main results)

This is the positive half of the study.  We isolate a *sharp, constructive*
sufficient condition for the canonical double cover of a Cayley digraph
`Cay(A, S)` to be unstable, and we specialise it to the even-order (cyclic)
case, which is the setting of the research mission.

## Main results

* `cayley_dc_unstable` — **abstract criterion.**  If `A` carries a parity
  character `χ : A → Bool` (an additive map onto `Bool` with `xor`) whose
  kernel contains the connection set `S`, then `Cay(A, S)` is unstable.  The
  explicit unexpected automorphism is `chiSwap χ : (a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)`.
* `cayley_dc_unstable_of_hom` — the same, phrased with a surjective additive
  homomorphism `f : A →+ ZMod 2`.
* `circulant_dc_unstable` — **even cyclic groups.**  For `2 ∣ n` and any
  connection set `S` lying in the even subgroup `ker(ℤ_n → ℤ₂)`, the circulant
  `Cay(ℤ_n, S)` is unstable.
* `circulant_dc_unstable_oddCap` — the **cross-domain bridge**: the same
  conclusion with "even order" packaged through the *Algebra*-domain parity
  predicate `oddCap` of `Algebra/ConformabilityOddOrder.lean`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Stage 1): the blanket claim "every even-order abelian Cayley
digraph is unstable".  Stage-2 brute force (`ComputationalEvidence.md`) shows
this is **false** (see `Boundary.lean`), but reveals a clean *true* core:
whenever the connection set `S` lies inside a parity-character kernel, the map
`(a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)` is an unexpected automorphism.

Experiment (Stage 2): we verified computationally (over ℤ₄, ℤ₆, ℤ₈) that
`chiSwap χ` is a genuine double-cover automorphism **iff** `χ(S) = {false}`,
i.e. `S ⊆ ker χ`, and that it is never of the expected form because `χ` is
surjective (so the layer-flip depends genuinely on the vertex).

Analysis (Stage 3): the proof needs exactly three algebraic facts about `χ`:
additivity (`hadd`), `χ 0 = false`, and surjectivity.  Additivity transports
"`q.1 - p.1 ∈ S`" (hence `χ(q.1 - p.1) = false`) into "`χ q.1 = χ p.1`", which
is what makes the layer-flip respect adjacency.  Surjectivity is what forbids
`chiSwap χ` from collapsing to a global deck flip `(a,i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)`.

Critique (Stage 4): the hypothesis `S ⊆ ker χ` makes `Cay(A,S)` disconnected
(it lives in the index-2 subgroup); this is the *honest* boundary of the
construction.  The complementary "bipartite" case `χ(S) = {true}` and the
genuinely connected stable examples are charted in `Boundary.lean`.

Bridge (Stage 5): `circulant_dc_unstable_oddCap` imports `oddCap` from the
**Algebra** domain (`Algebra/ConformabilityOddOrder.lean`) and combines it with
the **Applications/Combinatorics** double-cover construction here: the single
inequality `oddCap n < n` is exactly the even-order hypothesis `2 ∣ n ∧ 0 < n`
that powers the parity character, linking parity arithmetic to digraph
symmetry.
-/
import Mathlib
import Applications.CayleyDoubleCover.Core
import Algebra.ConformabilityOddOrder

namespace CayleyDoubleCover

variable {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A]

/-- **Abstract instability criterion.**
If `χ : A → Bool` is additive (with respect to `xor`), sends `0` to `false`,
is surjective onto `Bool`, and its kernel contains every element of `S`, then
`Cay(A, S)` is unstable: `chiSwap χ` is an unexpected automorphism of the
canonical double cover. -/
theorem cayley_dc_unstable
    (S : Finset A) (χ : A → Bool)
    (hadd : ∀ a b, χ (a + b) = xor (χ a) (χ b))
    (hzero : χ 0 = false)
    (hsurj : ∃ a, χ a = true)
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, χ s = false) :
    Unstable S := by
  refine ⟨chiSwap χ, ?_, ?_⟩
  · -- `chiSwap χ` preserves adjacency.
    intro p q
    simp only [DCadj, chiSwap_apply]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
      refine ⟨?_, h2⟩
      have hχ : χ q.1 = χ p.1 := by
        have hs := hker _ h2
        have key : χ (p.1 + (q.1 - p.1)) = xor (χ p.1) (χ (q.1 - p.1)) := hadd _ _
        rw [add_sub_cancel, hs] at key; simp [key]
      rw [hχ] at h1; revert h1; cases p.2 <;> cases q.2 <;> simp
    · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
      refine ⟨?_, h2⟩
      have hχ : χ q.1 = χ p.1 := by
        have hs := hker _ h2
        have key : χ (p.1 + (q.1 - p.1)) = xor (χ p.1) (χ (q.1 - p.1)) := hadd _ _
        rw [add_sub_cancel, hs] at key; simp [key]
      rw [hχ]; revert h1; cases p.2 <;> cases q.2 <;> simp
  · -- `chiSwap χ` is not of expected form.
    rintro ⟨σ, ε, h⟩
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hsurj
    have h0 := h (0, false)
    have ha2 := h (a, false)
    simp [hzero, ha] at h0 ha2
    rcases h0 with ⟨_, hε0⟩
    rcases ha2 with ⟨_, hε1⟩
    rw [hε0] at hε1; exact absurd hε1 (by decide)

/-- The parity character attached to an additive homomorphism `f : A →+ ZMod 2`. -/
def parityChar (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (a : A) : Bool := decide (f a = 1)

private lemma zmod2_add_xor :
    ∀ x y : ZMod 2, decide (x + y = 1) = xor (decide (x = 1)) (decide (y = 1)) := by
  decide

lemma parityChar_add (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (a b : A) :
    parityChar f (a + b) = xor (parityChar f a) (parityChar f b) := by
  unfold parityChar; rw [map_add]; exact zmod2_add_xor _ _

lemma parityChar_zero (f : A →+ ZMod 2) : parityChar f 0 = false := by
  unfold parityChar; rw [map_zero]; decide

lemma parityChar_surj (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (hf : Function.Surjective f) :
    ∃ a, parityChar f a = true := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hf 1
  exact ⟨a, by unfold parityChar; rw [ha]; decide⟩

/-- **Instability from a surjective additive character.**
If there is a surjective `f : A →+ ZMod 2` whose kernel contains `S`, then
`Cay(A, S)` is unstable. -/
theorem cayley_dc_unstable_of_hom
    (S : Finset A) (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (hf : Function.Surjective f)
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, f s = 0) :
    Unstable S := by
  refine cayley_dc_unstable S (parityChar f) (parityChar_add f) (parityChar_zero f)
    (parityChar_surj f hf) ?_
  intro s hs
  unfold parityChar; rw [hker s hs]; decide

/-- **Even cyclic groups (circulants).**
If `2 ∣ n` and every element of `S` lies in the even subgroup
`ker(ℤ_n → ℤ₂)`, then the circulant `Cay(ℤ_n, S)` is unstable. -/
theorem circulant_dc_unstable
    (n : ℕ) (h2 : (2 : ℕ) ∣ n) (S : Finset (ZMod n))
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, (ZMod.castHom h2 (ZMod 2)) s = 0) :
    Unstable S := by
  refine cayley_dc_unstable_of_hom S (ZMod.castHom h2 (ZMod 2)).toAddMonoidHom ?_ hker
  exact ZMod.castHom_surjective h2

/-- `oddCap n < n` is exactly the statement that `n` is a positive even number,
the even-order hypothesis we need.  (Algebra-domain bridge lemma.) -/
lemma two_dvd_of_oddCap_lt
    (n : ℕ) (hn : Catalog.Algebra.Conformability.oddCap n < n) : (2 : ℕ) ∣ n := by
  unfold Catalog.Algebra.Conformability.oddCap at hn
  split at hn
  · omega
  · rename_i h; rw [Nat.not_odd_iff_even] at h; exact h.two_dvd

/-- **Cross-domain bridge (Algebra ⊕ Applications/Combinatorics).**
The even-order hypothesis is packaged through the `Algebra`-domain parity
predicate `oddCap` of `Algebra/ConformabilityOddOrder.lean`: a positive integer
`n` is even precisely when `oddCap n < n`.  Here `oddCap` is genuinely
load-bearing — it is the *only* source of the divisibility `2 ∣ n` that builds
the parity character.  The connection set is required to consist of *even*
elements (`s = 2 • t`), i.e. to lie in the index-2 even subgroup; under that
hypothesis every such circulant is unstable. -/
theorem circulant_dc_unstable_oddCap
    (n : ℕ) (hn : Catalog.Algebra.Conformability.oddCap n < n)
    (S : Finset (ZMod n))
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, ∃ t : ZMod n, (2 : ZMod n) * t = s) :
    Unstable S := by
  have h2 : (2 : ℕ) ∣ n := two_dvd_of_oddCap_lt n hn
  refine circulant_dc_unstable n h2 S ?_
  intro s hs
  obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := hker s hs
  rw [← ht, map_mul]
  have : (ZMod.castHom h2 (ZMod 2)) 2 = 0 := by
    rw [map_ofNat]; decide
  rw [this, zero_mul]

end CayleyDoubleCover

# Computational Evidence: Stability of Cayley Digraphs and the `× K₂` Double Cover

All computations below were run by brute force (exhaustive permutation search)
over small abelian groups, *before* the Lean formalization, to decide whether
the mission's blanket claim is true and to locate the true core.

## Model

For `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` we build:
* the digraph `X` on `ℤₙ` with arc `a → b ⟺ (b − a) mod n ∈ S`;
* the canonical double cover `BX = X × K₂` on `ℤₙ × {0,1}` with arc
  `(a,i) → (b,j) ⟺ i ≠ j ∧ (b − a) mod n ∈ S`.

A digraph is **stable** iff `|Aut(BX)| = 2·|Aut(X)|` (the expected subgroup
`Aut(X) × ℤ₂` always embeds, so equality ⟺ no unexpected automorphism).

## 1. Exhaustive scan over `ℤ₂` and `ℤ₄`

Every `S ⊆ ℤ₄`, with `|Aut(X)|`, `|Aut(BX)|`, and verdict:

| S          | \|Aut X\| | \|Aut BX\| | verdict   | χ(S) parity |
|------------|----------:|-----------:|-----------|-------------|
| {}         | 24        | 40320      | unstable  | (empty)     |
| {0}        | 24        | 384        | unstable  | {0}         |
| {1}        | 4         | 32         | unstable  | {1}         |
| {2}        | 8         | 384        | unstable  | {0}         |
| {3}        | 4         | 32         | unstable  | {1}         |
| {0,1}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {0,2}      | 8         | 128        | unstable  | {0}         |
| {0,3}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {1,2}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {1,3}      | 8         | 128        | unstable  | {1}         |
| {2,3}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {0,1,2}    | 4         | 16         | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |
| {0,1,3}    | 8         | 48         | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |
| {0,2,3}    | 4         | 16         | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |
| {1,2,3}    | 24        | 48         | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {0,1,2,3}  | 24        | 1152       | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |

(All `S ⊆ ℤ₂` are unstable, but only via disconnected/bipartite double covers.)

### Key reads

* **Counterexample to the blanket claim.** `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is stable
  (`|Aut BX| = 8 = 2·4`). It is connected (`1` generates `ℤ₄`) and
  non-bipartite (loop `0 ∈ S`). ⇒ "even order ⇒ unstable" is **false**.
  This is the smallest counterexample; formalized in `Boundary.lean`.

* **True sufficient core.** Whenever the parity `χ(S) = {x mod 2 : x ∈ S}` is
  *constant* (all even, or all odd), the digraph is unstable in every row above.
  The "all even" case (`S` in the even subgroup) is proved in full generality
  in `Instability.lean` via the explicit automorphism `(a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)`.

* **Parity does not decide stability.** When `χ(S)` is *mixed*, both verdicts
  occur (`{0,1}` stable, `{0,1,2}` unstable). So stability is strictly subtler
  than connection-set parity.

## 2. Direct verification of the formal construction

For the construction `f(a,i) = (a, i ⊕ (a mod 2))` used in `Instability.lean`,
we checked over `ℤ₄, ℤ₆, ℤ₈` that `f` is a genuine double-cover automorphism and
is never of the expected form, **exactly** when `S` lies in the even subgroup:

```
n=4 S=[0,2]   chi(S)={0}  f_is_aut=True   f_expected=False  => unstable witness
n=4 S=[1,3]   chi(S)={1}  f_is_aut=False                    => (needs other witness)
n=6 S=[0,2,4] chi(S)={0}  f_is_aut=True   f_expected=False  => unstable witness
n=6 S=[2,4]   chi(S)={0}  f_is_aut=True   f_expected=False  => unstable witness
n=8 S=[0,2,4,6] chi(S)={0} f_is_aut=True f_expected=False   => unstable witness
```

This confirms the precise hypothesis `S ⊆ ker χ` of `cayley_dc_unstable`, and
shows the construction breaks (`f_is_aut=False`) once `S` leaves the kernel —
matching the theoretical analysis.

## 3. OEIS

No single OEIS sequence governs `|Aut(BX)|` across `S`; the orders depend on the
full subset structure rather than only on `|S|`, so no sequence match is
reported. (The stable subsets of `ℤ₄` — count 5 — are too short to fingerprint.)

# Future Directions — Stability of Cayley Digraphs and the `× K₂` Double Cover

Derived from this cycle's findings (`Core.lean`, `Instability.lean`,
`Boundary.lean`, `ComputationalEvidence.md`). The headline discovery is that the
blanket conjecture — *"every even-order abelian Cayley digraph is unstable"* —
is **false** (`Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is stable), while a sharp constructive sufficient
condition (`S` inside a parity-character kernel) is true in full generality.

---

### Conjecture 1 — Parity-kernel characterisation for connected circulants
For a **connected** circulant `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` with `n` even, it is unstable
**iff** there is a surjective homomorphism `χ : ℤₙ → ℤ₂` with `S ⊆ ker χ`
*or* a twin/blow-up obstruction; equivalently the only "elementary" source of
instability is the parity kernel.

*The key insight is...* that in every computed row the parity-kernel witness
`(a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)` already accounts for all *constant-parity* instability,
so the residual unstable mixed-parity cases must come from a structurally
different (twin/quotient) mechanism, which the conjecture isolates.

*Why now?* We already have the kernel direction fully formalized
(`cayley_dc_unstable`) and a decidable stability checker (`Boundary.lean`); the
converse can be attacked one `n` at a time by `native_decide` to build evidence
before a general proof.

---

### Conjecture 2 — Every finite abelian group of even order admits the witness
For **every** finite abelian group `A` of even order there is a surjective
additive homomorphism `χ : A → ℤ₂`; hence `cayley_dc_unstable` applies to *all*
connection sets contained in some index-2 subgroup, not just cyclic ones.

*The key insight is...* that `2 ∣ |A|` forces `A/2A ≠ 0` (equivalently a nonzero
`2`-torsion quotient), and any nonzero elementary-abelian `2`-quotient surjects
onto `ℤ₂`, so the character `χ` of `Instability.lean` always exists.

*Why now?* The cyclic instance is done via `ZMod.castHom`; the general case only
needs the existence lemma `∃ f : A →+ ZMod 2, Surjective f`, a self-contained
group-theory target that immediately upgrades `circulant_dc_unstable` to all
abelian groups.

---

### Conjecture 3 — The "bipartite" twin of the kernel construction
If a surjective `χ : A → ℤ₂` has `S ⊆ A ∖ ker χ` (every generator is *odd*,
the bipartite case), then `Cay(A, S)` is again unstable, witnessed by
translating one connected component of the double cover by a nonzero element of
`ker χ` while fixing the other.

*The key insight is...* that the invariant `J(a,i) = i ⊕ χ(a)` is constant along
arcs when `χ(S) = {1}`, so the double cover splits into two components that can
be moved independently — an automorphism that is provably unexpected whenever
`|ker χ| ≥ 2`.

*Why now?* The computational table shows every all-odd `S` is unstable, and the
component-translation map is as explicit as `chiSwap`; only the
"unexpectedness" bookkeeping remains, mirroring the proof already in
`Instability.lean`.

---

### Conjecture 4 — Stability is `coNP`-flavoured but parity-blind
Deciding stability of `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` is **not** a function of `(n, |S|, χ(S))`
alone: there exist `n` and two sets `S, S'` with the same size and same parity
multiset, one stable and one unstable.

*The key insight is...* that `{0,1,2}` (unstable) and a same-parity-profile
mixed set can already diverge at `n = 4`, so any efficient stability test must
read finer structure (e.g. the Fourier support of `1_S`), not just coarse parity
statistics.

*Why now?* The decidable model in `Core.lean` lets us mine `n ≤ 12` exhaustively
for minimal "parity-twin" pairs, turning the conjecture into a finite search
that can seed an invariant-based classification.

---

### Conjecture 5 — Fourier criterion bridging to additive combinatorics
Instability of `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` (n even) is controlled by the value of the
order-`2` additive character `ψ(x) = stdAddChar(n/2 · x)` on `S`: if `ψ` is
constant on `S` then `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` is unstable.

*The key insight is...* that `ψ(s) = +1 ⟺ s` is even `⟺ χ(s) = false`, so the
parity-kernel hypothesis of `Instability.lean` is *exactly* a statement about a
single Fourier character — directly linking double-cover stability to the
`ZMod.dft` toolkit of `Combinatorics/FourierFiniteGroups.lean`.

*Why now?* Both ingredients already exist in the catalog (the parity character
here, `stdAddChar` and orthogonality there); proving `ψ(s) = 1 ↔ χ(s) = false`
is the one bridge lemma needed to restate all instability results spectrally.

The union of all such lines is the **bush** `B = ⋃_{m∈F} L m`.  We prove the
exact count

which is the model statement that "the bush is essentially all of the plane":
it occupies a positive proportion `1 − 1/q + 1/q²` of the `q²` points.  This is

/-- The line through the origin of slope `m`: `{(x, m·x) : x ∈ F}`. -/
def line (m : F) : Finset (F × F) := Finset.univ.image (fun x : F => (x, m * x))

/-- The bush: the union of all lines through the origin. -/
def bush (F : Type*) [Field F] [Fintype F] [DecidableEq F] : Finset (F × F) :=
  Finset.univ.biUnion (fun m : F => line m)

/-- Characterization of the bush: it is exactly the set of points with nonzero
first coordinate, together with the origin. -/
theorem bush_eq :
    bush F = (Finset.univ.filter (fun p : F × F => p.1 ≠ 0 ∨ p = (0, 0))) := by
  ext ⟨a, b⟩
  simp only [bush, line, mem_biUnion, mem_univ, mem_image, true_and, mem_filter,

axis `{(0, b) : b ≠ 0}`, which has `q − 1` points.

  rw [ Finset.card_eq_sum_ones ];
  rw [ show ( Finset.filter ( fun x : F × F => x.1 = 0 ∧ ¬x = ( 0, 0 ) ) Finset.univ : Finset ( F × F ) ) = Finset.image ( fun x : F => ( 0, x ) ) ( Finset.univ.erase 0 ) from ?_, Finset.sum_image ] <;> norm_num;

`q² − q + 1` points, where `q = |F|`.
-/

/-!
# Kakeya in finite-field model: the bush of lines through the origin

This file develops a rigorous, fully-proved fragment of the *finite-field model*
of the Kakeya problem.  The full Kakeya conjecture (a Besicovitch set in `ℝ^n`
has Hausdorff dimension `n`) is far out of reach of current formalization, so we
work in the discrete model `F²` for a finite field `F`, which is the setting of
the Wolff / Dvir / Katz–Tao line of work.

A *line through the origin* with slope `m` is `L m = {(x, m·x) : x ∈ F}`.
The union of all such lines is the **bush** `B = ⋃_{m∈F} L m`.  We prove the
exact count

  `|B| = q² − q + 1`,  where `q = |F|`,

which is the model statement that "the bush is essentially all of the plane":
it occupies a positive proportion `1 − 1/q + 1/q²` of the `q²` points.  This is
the discrete analogue of the fact that a Kakeya set has full dimension.

We also prove the basic incidence fact that two lines of *distinct slope* meet
in exactly one point, the combinatorial engine behind every Kakeya lower bound.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): in the finite-field plane the union of the `q` lines
  through the origin should already contain almost every point, namely all `(a,b)`
  with `a ≠ 0` plus the single point `(0,0)`.  Predicted count `q² − q + 1`.
* Experiment (Experimenter): formalized the bush as a `Finset.biUnion` of images
  and proved the set equality `bush = {p | p.1 ≠ 0 ∨ p = 0}` by solving
  `m = b / a` when `a ≠ 0` (field arithmetic, `field_simp`).
* Analysis (Analyst): the count reduces to removing the `q − 1` "vertical-axis
  off-origin" points `(0, b)`, `b ≠ 0`, from the full `q²` points.  The argument
  is purely combinatorial once the set equality is known.
* Critique (Critic): the theorem is non-trivial (genuine set equality + counting,
  uses `field_simp`, `card_sdiff`, a bijection), not a definitional `rfl`.  Edge
  case `q = 1` (the field `F₁` does not exist, smallest field has `q = 2`) is fine:
  natural-number subtraction `q² − q + 1` is exact for `q ≥ 1`.
* Synthesis (PI): `bush_card` is the headline result; `line_distinct_slope_inter`
  is the reusable incidence lemma feeding future Kakeya lower bounds.
-/

open Finset

namespace KakeyaBush

variable {F : Type*} [Field F] [Fintype F] [DecidableEq F]

/-- The line through the origin of slope `m`: `{(x, m·x) : x ∈ F}`. -/
def line (m : F) : Finset (F × F) := Finset.univ.image (fun x : F => (x, m * x))

/-- The bush: the union of all lines through the origin. -/
def bush (F : Type*) [Field F] [Fintype F] [DecidableEq F] : Finset (F × F) :=
  Finset.univ.biUnion (fun m : F => line m)

/-- Characterization of the bush: it is exactly the set of points with nonzero
first coordinate, together with the origin. -/
theorem bush_eq :
    bush F = (Finset.univ.filter (fun p : F × F => p.1 ≠ 0 ∨ p = (0, 0))) := by
  ext ⟨a, b⟩
  simp only [bush, line, mem_biUnion, mem_univ, mem_image, true_and, mem_filter,
    Prod.ext_iff]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨m, x, rfl, rfl⟩
    by_cases h : x = 0
    · subst h; right; exact ⟨rfl, by simp⟩
    · left; exact h
  · rintro (ha | ⟨ha, hb⟩)
    · exact ⟨b / a, a, ⟨rfl, by field_simp⟩⟩
    · exact ⟨0, 0, ⟨ha.symm, by simp [hb]⟩⟩

/-
The "bad" set removed from the full plane: off-origin points of the vertical
axis `{(0, b) : b ≠ 0}`, which has `q − 1` points.
-/
theorem bad_card :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun p : F × F => p.1 = 0 ∧ p ≠ (0, 0))).card
      = Fintype.card F - 1 := by
  rw [ Finset.card_eq_sum_ones ];
  rw [ show ( Finset.filter ( fun x : F × F => x.1 = 0 ∧ ¬x = ( 0, 0 ) ) Finset.univ : Finset ( F × F ) ) = Finset.image ( fun x : F => ( 0, x ) ) ( Finset.univ.erase 0 ) from ?_, Finset.sum_image ] <;> norm_num;
  grind

/-
**Bush count.** The bush of lines through the origin in `F²` has exactly
`q² − q + 1` points, where `q = |F|`.
-/
theorem bush_card :
    (bush F).card = Fintype.card F * Fintype.card F - Fintype.card F + 1 := by
  rw [ bush_eq, tsub_add_eq_add_tsub ];
  · convert Finset.card_univ_diff ( Finset.univ.filter fun p : F × F => p.1 = 0 ∧ p ≠ ( 0, 0 ) ) using 1;
    · exact congr_arg _ ( by ext; by_cases h : ‹F × F›.1 = 0 <;> by_cases h' : ‹F × F› = ( 0, 0 ) <;> simp +decide [ h, h' ] );
    · rw [ Fintype.card_prod, bad_card ];
      rw [ Nat.sub_eq_of_eq_add ];
      linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show 1 ≤ Fintype.card F from Fintype.card_pos ), Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show Fintype.card F - 1 ≤ Fintype.card F * Fintype.card F from Nat.sub_le_of_le_add <| by nlinarith ) ];
  · nlinarith

/-- **Incidence lemma.** Two lines through the origin of distinct slopes meet only
at the origin. -/
theorem line_distinct_slope_inter {m₁ m₂ : F} (h : m₁ ≠ m₂) :
    line m₁ ∩ line m₂ = {(0, 0)} := by
  ext p
  simp only [line, mem_inter, mem_image, mem_univ, true_and, mem_singleton]
  constructor <;> intro hp <;> aesop

/-- A *Kakeya set* in the through-origin model: a set containing a full line of
every slope through the origin. -/
def IsKakeyaSet (K : Finset (F × F)) : Prop := ∀ m : F, line m ⊆ K

/-- **Kakeya lower bound (finite-field, through-origin model).** Any Kakeya set in
`F²` has at least `q² − q + 1` points: it must contain the whole bush. -/
theorem card_ge_of_isKakeyaSet {K : Finset (F × F)} (hK : IsKakeyaSet K) :
    Fintype.card F * Fintype.card F - Fintype.card F + 1 ≤ K.card := by
  rw [← bush_card]
  exact Finset.card_le_card (Finset.biUnion_subset.mpr fun m _ => hK m)

end KakeyaBush

# The additive-combinatorics bridge: sumset growth (Katz–Tao framework)

The Katz–Tao approach to the Kakeya problem reduces dimension lower bounds to
*sum–difference* estimates in additive combinatorics: a Kakeya set forces a
configuration whose iterated sumsets must grow, and quantitative growth
translates back into a dimension bound.  The cleanest exactly-provable engine of
this kind is the **Cauchy–Davenport** inequality in the prime cyclic group
`ZMod p`.

This file proves the iterated-sumset growth law that powers such arguments:

  `|kA| ≥ min(p, k·(|A| − 1) + 1)`  for every nonempty `A ⊆ ZMod p`,

by induction on `k` using Cauchy–Davenport, and deduces the qualitative
corollary that any set with at least two elements *generates the whole group*
under enough additions (`kA = ZMod p` once `k ≥ p − 1`).  This is the discrete
analogue of "a Kakeya set, after enough additive combination, fills space".

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): Cauchy–Davenport should iterate to a linear-in-`k`
  growth `|kA| ≳ k|A|` until saturation at `p`.  Predicted exact bound
  `min(p, k(|A|−1)+1)`.
* Experiment (Experimenter): defined `sumIter A k` by recursion (`A + (A + …)`),
  proved nonemptiness by induction, and ran the induction on `k`, feeding
  `ZMod.cauchy_davenport` at each step.  The `min` and `ℕ`-subtraction bookkeeping
  was the only real obstacle (handled with `omega`).
* Analysis (Analyst): the bound is sharp for arithmetic progressions
  (`A = {0,1,…,m−1}` gives `kA = {0,…,k(m−1)}` of size exactly `k(m−1)+1` while
  that stays `< p`).  Saturation happens at `k = ⌈(p−1)/(|A|−1)⌉`.
* Critique (Critic): the corollary `sumset_generates` is non-vacuous — it needs
  `|A| ≥ 2`; for `|A| = 1` (singleton) `kA` is a singleton forever, which the
  bound `min(p, k·0+1) = 1` correctly predicts.  No hidden triviality: the proof
  uses genuine induction and Cauchy–Davenport, not `decide`.
* Synthesis (PI): `card_sumIter_ge` is the headline growth law;
  `sumset_generates` is the saturation corollary tying it to "filling space".
-/

open Finset Pointwise

namespace KakeyaKatzTao

/-- Iterated sumset: `sumIter A k = A + A + ⋯ + A` (`k+1` copies, so
`sumIter A 0 = A`). -/
def sumIter {p : ℕ} (A : Finset (ZMod p)) : ℕ → Finset (ZMod p)
  | 0 => A
  | (k + 1) => A + sumIter A k

@[simp] theorem sumIter_zero {p : ℕ} (A : Finset (ZMod p)) : sumIter A 0 = A := rfl

theorem sumIter_succ {p : ℕ} (A : Finset (ZMod p)) (k : ℕ) :
    sumIter A (k + 1) = A + sumIter A k := rfl

/-
The iterated sumset of a nonempty set is nonempty.
-/
theorem sumIter_nonempty {p : ℕ} {A : Finset (ZMod p)} (hA : A.Nonempty) (k : ℕ) :
    (sumIter A k).Nonempty := by
  induction' k with k ih <;> simp_all +decide [ sumIter_succ ]

/-
Any subset of `ZMod p` has at most `p` elements.
-/
theorem card_le_p {p : ℕ} [NeZero p] (A : Finset (ZMod p)) : A.card ≤ p := by
  simpa using Finset.card_le_univ A

/-
**Iterated Cauchy–Davenport growth.** For a prime `p` and nonempty
`A ⊆ ZMod p`, the `k`-fold sumset satisfies `|kA| ≥ min(p, k(|A|−1)+1)`.
-/
theorem card_sumIter_ge {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) {A : Finset (ZMod p)}
    (hA : A.Nonempty) (k : ℕ) :
    min p (k * (A.card - 1) + 1) ≤ (sumIter A k).card := by
  induction' k with k ih;
  · grind +suggestions;
  · have := @ZMod.cauchy_davenport;
    convert this hp hA ( sumIter_nonempty hA k ) |> le_trans _ using 1;
    grind

/-
**Saturation / generation.** If `A ⊆ ZMod p` has at least two elements, then
once `k ≥ p − 1` the iterated sumset is all of `ZMod p` (it has `p` elements).
-/
theorem sumset_generates {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) {A : Finset (ZMod p)}
    (hA : 2 ≤ A.card) {k : ℕ} (hk : p - 1 ≤ k) :
    (sumIter A k).card = p := by
  refine' le_antisymm _ _;
  · haveI := Fact.mk hp; exact le_trans ( Finset.card_le_univ _ ) ( by simp +decide ) ;
  · refine' le_trans _ ( card_sumIter_ge hp ( Finset.card_pos.mp ( by linarith ) ) k );
    exact le_min le_rfl ( by nlinarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel hp.pos, Nat.sub_pos_of_lt hA ] )

end KakeyaKatzTao

# Future Directions — EML Fixed-Point Dynamics

Derived from this research cycle (`EML/FixedPointRate.lean`,
`EML/FixedPointConcreteInstance.lean`), which upgraded the EML fixed-point story
from "converges" to "converges with a certified, computable geometric rate
`O(ρⁿ)`" and exhibited an explicit non-vacuous contraction instance.

---

## D1. The contraction ratio is asymptotically *exactly* `|f'(x*)|`

**Conjecture.** For an `EMLContractionData D` with fixed point `x*`, the *true*
asymptotic convergence ratio equals `|f'(x*)| = exp(a)·b / (b·x* + c)`, in the
sense that `|xₙ₊₁ − x*| / |xₙ − x*| → |f'(x*)|`, and this limit can be strictly
smaller than the certified envelope ratio `D.rho`.

*The key insight is that* the global Lipschitz constant `D.rho` only upper-bounds
the *local* multiplier at the fixed point, so the honest rate is a derivative
evaluated at `x*`, recoverable from the mean value theorem already used to build
the contraction.

*Why now?* `FixedPointRate.lean` proves the `O(ρⁿ)` envelope but treats `ρ` as an
external certificate; the next natural sharpening is to identify the *optimal* `ρ`
as the spectral data `|f'(x*)|`, which the existing `EMLIterOp.deriv_eq` already
makes available symbolically.

---

## D2. A posteriori (residual) error control

**Conjecture.** The EML iteration admits the a-posteriori bound
`|xₙ − x*| ≤ ρ/(1−ρ) · |xₙ − xₙ₋₁|`, giving a *computable stopping criterion*
from two consecutive iterates without knowing `x*` in advance.

*The key insight is that* the same geometric-tail argument behind the a-priori
estimate, re-anchored at step `n` instead of step `0`, converts the last observed
step length into a rigorous remaining-error certificate.

*Why now?* The a-priori bound `iterSeq_error_bound` needs `|x₁ − x₀|`; for
practical EML iterative algorithms one wants a *runtime* certificate, which the a
posteriori form supplies directly and is a short reindexing away.

---

## D3. Smooth (analytic) dependence of `x*` on the parameter `a`

**Conjecture.** For fixed `b, c` in the contraction regime, the fixed point
`x*(a)` is a real-analytic function of `a`, with `dx*/da = x* / (1 − f'(x*))` and
a convergent Maclaurin series whose radius of convergence is the largest `a` for
which `|f'(x*(a))| < 1`.

*The key insight is that* the implicit equation `x* = exp(a)·log(b·x*+c)` has
non-vanishing partial derivative `1 − f'(x*) ≠ 0` precisely on the contraction
regime, so the analytic implicit function theorem applies.

*Why now?* The existing `fixedPoint_powerSeries_conjecture` only secured
*existence* of a fixed point via IVT; with the contraction machinery now in place,
the implicit-function route to genuine analytic dependence (and the series the
mission asked for) becomes reachable.

---

## D4. Sharp characterisation of the invariant-interval / small-`c` boundary

**Conjecture.** For `b = 1` and `c ∈ (0,1)`, no closed interval inside the domain
`{x : x + c > 0}` is simultaneously `f`-invariant *and* contracting unless it is
pushed to `x`-values with `x + c > 1`; equivalently, the set of `(a,c)` admitting
an EML contraction interval is exactly `{(a,c) : exp(a) < (b·x*+c)/b at the
relevant fixed point}` and excludes a wedge near `c → 0⁺`.

*The key insight is that* `log` changes sign at argument `1`, so for tiny `c` the
operator maps part of any left-anchored interval below `0`, breaking self-mapping;
the boundary is governed by where `f` crosses the diagonal with slope `< 1`.

*Why now?* The computational evidence (`ComputationalEvidence.md`) shows the
mission's literal `c ∈ (0,1)` test case is dynamically delicate; mapping out the
exact admissible region turns that obstruction into a clean theorem.

---

## D5. Composition (deep EML) preserves geometric convergence

**Conjecture.** A finite composition `f_k ∘ ... ∘ f_1` of EML operators, each a
contraction with ratio `ρᵢ` on a common invariant interval, is itself a
contraction with ratio `∏ ρᵢ`, and its iteration converges at rate `O((∏ρᵢ)ⁿ)`.

*The key insight is that* Lipschitz constants multiply under composition, so the
single-operator `lipschitz_of_deriv_bound` lemma tensors up to depth without new
analysis — connecting this fixed-point theory to the deep-network theme of
`EML/DeepComposition.lean`.

*Why now?* `FixedPointRate.lean` isolates the rate from the analytic content; that
separation is exactly what makes the multi-layer (deep EML) generalisation a
formal corollary rather than a fresh project.

# Deligne's bound: Frobenius eigenvalues are Weil numbers (GL₂ over ℚ)

This file formalizes the **analytic half of the GL₂ Langlands data over `ℚ`**: Deligne's
theorem (the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for weight-`2` newforms), which says that the
Frobenius eigenvalues attached to a Hecke eigenform are **Weil numbers of weight one**.
Concretely, the two roots `α, β` of the Hecke polynomial `X² − a_p·X + p`
(from `Catalog.Novelty.EichlerShimuraGL2`) satisfy
$$|\alpha| = |\beta| = \sqrt p,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad |a_p| \le 2\sqrt p .$$

This is the GL₂ refinement of the GL₁ picture in the catalog: there the local Frobenius
value is a *root of unity* (`|·| = 1`); here it is a Weil number of absolute value `√p`,
and the new phenomenon is that the bound is a genuine inequality controlled by the
discriminant of the quadratic Hecke polynomial.

Main results:

* `DeligneBoundGL2.deligne_bound_iff` — the scalar Deligne bound
  `|a| ≤ 2√p ↔ a² ≤ 4p`.
* `DeligneBoundGL2.deligne_root_abs` — every complex root of the Hecke polynomial is a
  Weil number: if `a² ≤ 4p` and `(heckePoly a p).eval z = 0`, then `‖z‖ = √p`.
* `DeligneBoundGL2.deligne_weil_pair` — the two Frobenius eigenvalues `α, β` satisfy
  `αβ = p` and `‖α‖ = ‖β‖ = √p`.
* `DeligneBoundGL2.deligne_frob_eigenvalues` — the eigenvalues of the concrete Frobenius
  companion matrix `frobMatrix a p` (over `ℂ`) all have absolute value `√p`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the catalog GL(1) datum is a root of unity, `|·| = 1`.  The bold
GL₂ analogue, and the deepest input to the correspondence, is Deligne's bound: the Frobenius
eigenvalues lie on the circle of radius `√p`.  Conjecture: the *purely real-algebraic core* of
this — "a real quadratic `z² − a z + p` with `p > 0` has all complex roots on `|z| = √p` exactly
when `a² ≤ 4p`" — is provable unconditionally and is the honest finite shadow of Deligne's
theorem (whose full proof needs the Weil conjectures).

Experiment (Experimenter): the equivalence `|a| ≤ 2√p ↔ a² ≤ 4p` is `nlinarith` after rewriting
`4p = (2√p)²` via `Real.sq_sqrt`.  For the root statement we split a complex root `z = x + yi`
into real/imaginary parts (`congrArg Complex.re/im`), giving `2xy = ay` and `x² − y² − ax + p = 0`.
Case `y = 0`: the discriminant `(2x − a)² = a² − 4p ≤ 0` forces `a² = 4p`, hence `x² = p`.
Case `y ≠ 0`: `2x = a`, and substituting collapses `x² + y² = p`.  Either way `normSq z = p`,
so `‖z‖ = √p`.  The pair statement and the companion-matrix statement reuse `deligne_root_abs`.

Analysis (Analyst): the hypothesis `a² ≤ 4p` is *exactly* the boundary between Weil numbers and
real Frobenius eigenvalues.  When `a² > 4p` the roots are real with distinct moduli — the bound
fails — so the hypothesis is load-bearing, mirroring why Deligne's theorem is a real theorem and
not a formality.  The case split `y = 0` vs `y ≠ 0` is the formal trace of "ordinary vs
supersingular / split vs inert" behavior of the local datum.

Critique (Critic): is any result trivial?  No — `deligne_root_abs` is a genuine case analysis
on the geometry of the root, not `decide`/`simp`.  `deligne_frob_eigenvalues` is not vacuous:

`p = 0` is excluded (`0 < p`) since a Weil number of weight one needs `p > 0`; at `a² = 4p`
the two eigenvalues coincide at `±√p`, still satisfying the conclusion.

Weil bound) gives both halves of the local GL₂ correspondence over `ℚ`: a `2 × 2` Frobenius with
trace `a_p`, determinant `p`, Eichler–Shimura relation, and Weil eigenvalues of absolute value

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Novelty.EichlerShimuraGL2

open Polynomial Matrix EichlerShimuraGL2

namespace DeligneBoundGL2

/-- **Deligne's bound, scalar form.** For `p ≥ 0`, the Hecke eigenvalue bound `|a| ≤ 2√p`
is equivalent to the discriminant condition `a² ≤ 4p`. -/
theorem deligne_bound_iff (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 ≤ p) :
    |a| ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt p ↔ a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p := by
  have key : (2 * Real.sqrt p) ^ 2 = 4 * p := by rw [mul_pow, Real.sq_sqrt hp]; ring
  constructor
  · intro h; nlinarith [sq_abs a, h, abs_nonneg a, Real.sqrt_nonneg p, key]
  · intro h; nlinarith [sq_abs a, h, abs_nonneg a, Real.sqrt_nonneg p, key]

/-- **Deligne / Ramanujan–Petersson (weight-one Weil bound).** Every complex root of the Hecke
polynomial `X² − a·X + p` is a Weil number of absolute value `√p`, provided `a² ≤ 4p`. -/
theorem deligne_root_abs (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 < p) (ha : a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p) (z : ℂ)
    (hz : (heckePoly (a : ℂ) (p : ℂ)).eval z = 0) : ‖z‖ = Real.sqrt p := by
  rw [heckePoly_eval] at hz
  have hre : z.re ^ 2 - z.im ^ 2 - a * z.re + p = 0 := by
    have h := congrArg Complex.re hz
    simp [Complex.add_re, Complex.sub_re, Complex.mul_re, pow_two] at h
    linarith [h]
  have him : 2 * z.re * z.im - a * z.im = 0 := by
    have h := congrArg Complex.im hz
    simp [Complex.add_im, Complex.sub_im, Complex.mul_im, pow_two] at h
    linarith [h]
  have hns : Complex.normSq z = p := by
    rw [Complex.normSq_apply]
    rcases eq_or_ne z.im 0 with hy | hy
    · rw [hy] at hre ⊢
      have h1 : z.re ^ 2 - a * z.re + p = 0 := by ring_nf; ring_nf at hre; linarith
      nlinarith [sq_nonneg (2 * z.re - a)]
    · have hx : a = 2 * z.re := by
        have h0 : z.im * (a - 2 * z.re) = 0 := by ring_nf; nlinarith [him]
        rcases mul_eq_zero.1 h0 with h | h
        · exact absurd h hy
        · linarith
      subst hx
      nlinarith [hre]
  rw [Complex.norm_def, hns]

/-- **The Weil pair.** The two Frobenius eigenvalues `α, β` (roots of the Hecke polynomial)
satisfy `αβ = p` and both have absolute value `√p`. -/
theorem deligne_weil_pair (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 < p) (ha : a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p) (α β : ℂ)
    (hsum : α + β = (a : ℂ)) (hprod : α * β = (p : ℂ)) :
    α * β = (p : ℂ) ∧ ‖α‖ = Real.sqrt p ∧ ‖β‖ = Real.sqrt p := by
  refine ⟨hprod, ?_, ?_⟩ <;>
    · apply deligne_root_abs a p hp ha
      rw [heckePoly_eval, ← hsum, ← hprod]; ring

/-- **Frobenius eigenvalues are Weil numbers.** Any eigenvalue `λ` of the concrete Frobenius
companion matrix `frobMatrix a p` over `ℂ` (i.e. with `frobMatrix a p − λ` singular) has
absolute value `√p`, whenever `a² ≤ 4p`. -/
theorem deligne_frob_eigenvalues (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 < p) (ha : a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p) (lam : ℂ)
    (hlam : ¬ IsUnit (frobMatrix (a : ℂ) (p : ℂ) - lam • (1 : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℂ))) :
    ‖lam‖ = Real.sqrt p := by
  apply deligne_root_abs a p hp ha
  -- `λ` is an eigenvalue iff `det(frobMatrix − λ) = 0`, which equals `heckePoly` evaluated at `λ`.
  have hdet : Matrix.det (frobMatrix (a : ℂ) (p : ℂ) - lam • (1 : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℂ)) = 0 := by
    by_contra hne
    exact hlam ((Matrix.isUnit_iff_isUnit_det _).mpr (isUnit_iff_ne_zero.mpr hne))
  have hmat : frobMatrix (a : ℂ) (p : ℂ) - lam • (1 : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℂ)
      = !![-lam, -(p : ℂ); 1, (a : ℂ) - lam] := by
    ext i j; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp [frobMatrix]
  rw [hmat, Matrix.det_fin_two_of] at hdet
  rw [heckePoly_eval]
  linear_combination hdet

end DeligneBoundGL2

import Catalog.Novelty.EichlerShimuraGL2

open Polynomial Matrix EichlerShimuraGL2

namespace DeligneBoundGL2

/-- **Deligne's bound, scalar form.** For `p ≥ 0`, the Hecke eigenvalue bound `|a| ≤ 2√p`
is equivalent to the discriminant condition `a² ≤ 4p`. -/
theorem deligne_bound_iff (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 ≤ p) :
    |a| ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt p ↔ a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p := by
  have key : (2 * Real.sqrt p) ^ 2 = 4 * p := by rw [mul_pow, Real.sq_sqrt hp]; ring
  constructor
  · intro h; nlinarith [sq_abs a, h, abs_nonneg a, Real.sqrt_nonneg p, key]
  · intro h; nlinarith [sq_abs a, h, abs_nonneg a, Real.sqrt_nonneg p, key]

/-- **Deligne / Ramanujan–Petersson (weight-one Weil bound).** Every complex root of the Hecke
polynomial `X² − a·X + p` is a Weil number of absolute value `√p`, provided `a² ≤ 4p`. -/
theorem deligne_root_abs (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 < p) (ha : a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p) (z : ℂ)
    (hz : (heckePoly (a : ℂ) (p : ℂ)).eval z = 0) : ‖z‖ = Real.sqrt p := by
  rw [heckePoly_eval] at hz
  have hre : z.re ^ 2 - z.im ^ 2 - a * z.re + p = 0 := by
    have h := congrArg Complex.re hz
    simp [Complex.add_re, Complex.sub_re, Complex.mul_re, pow_two] at h
    linarith [h]
  have him : 2 * z.re * z.im - a * z.im = 0 := by
    have h := congrArg Complex.im hz
    simp [Complex.add_im, Complex.sub_im, Complex.mul_im, pow_two] at h
    linarith [h]
  have hns : Complex.normSq z = p := by
    rw [Complex.normSq_apply]
    rcases eq_or_ne z.im 0 with hy | hy
    · rw [hy] at hre ⊢
      have h1 : z.re ^ 2 - a * z.re + p = 0 := by ring_nf; ring_nf at hre; linarith
      nlinarith [sq_nonneg (2 * z.re - a)]
    · have hx : a = 2 * z.re := by
        have h0 : z.im * (a - 2 * z.re) = 0 := by ring_nf; nlinarith [him]
        rcases mul_eq_zero.1 h0 with h | h
        · exact absurd h hy
        · linarith
      subst hx
      nlinarith [hre]
  rw [Complex.norm_def, hns]

/-- **The Weil pair.** The two Frobenius eigenvalues `α, β` (roots of the Hecke polynomial)
satisfy `αβ = p` and both have absolute value `√p`. -/
theorem deligne_weil_pair (a p : ℝ) (hp : 0 < p) (ha : a ^ 2 ≤ 4 * p) (α β : ℂ)
    (hsum : α + β = (a : ℂ)) (hprod : α * β = (p : ℂ)) :
    α * β = (p : ℂ) ∧ ‖α‖ = Real.sqrt p ∧ ‖β‖ = Real.sqrt p := by
  refine ⟨hprod, ?_, ?_⟩ <;>
    · apply deligne_root_abs a p hp ha
      rw [heckePoly_eval, ← hsum, ← hprod]; ring

absolute value `√p`, whenever `a² ≤ 4p`. -/

    by_contra hne

    ext i j; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp [frobMatrix]
  rw [hmat, Matrix.det_fin_two_of] at hdet
  rw [heckePoly_eval]
  linear_combination hdet

end DeligneBoundGL2

import Mathlib

open Polynomial Matrix

namespace EichlerShimuraGL2

/-- The Hecke / Frobenius characteristic polynomial `X² − a·X + b`.
For a weight-2 eigenform, `a` is the Hecke eigenvalue `a_p` and `b` is the prime `p`. -/
noncomputable def heckePoly {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a b : R) : R[X] := X ^ 2 - C a * X + C b

@[simp] lemma heckePoly_eval {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a b r : R) :
    (heckePoly a b).eval r = r ^ 2 - a * r + b := by
  simp [heckePoly]

/-- **Eichler–Shimura congruence relation** (rank-2 Cayley–Hamilton):
`Frob² = T·Frob − p`, where the Hecke operator `T` is the trace and `p` the determinant. -/
theorem eichlerShimura {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (M : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) R) :
    M * M = (Matrix.trace M) • M - (Matrix.det M) • (1 : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) R) := by
  ext i j
  fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;>
    simp [Matrix.mul_apply, Fin.sum_univ_two, Matrix.trace_fin_two, Matrix.det_fin_two] <;> ring

/-- Vieta: the Hecke polynomial factors through its Frobenius eigenvalues `α, β`. -/
theorem heckePoly_factor {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a b α β : R)
    (hs : α + β = a) (hp : α * β = b) :
    heckePoly a b = (X - C α) * (X - C β) := by
  subst hs hp; simp only [heckePoly, C_add, C_mul]; ring

/-- The local Euler factor `1 − a·X + b·X²` factors through the Frobenius eigenvalues. -/
theorem eulerFactor_factor {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a b α β : R)
    (hs : α + β = a) (hp : α * β = b) :
    (1 - C a * X + C b * X ^ 2 : R[X]) = (1 - C α * X) * (1 - C β * X) := by
  subst hs hp; simp only [C_add, C_mul]; ring

/-- The **Frobenius companion matrix** with trace `a` and determinant `p`:
a concrete realization of the local Frobenius datum. -/
def frobMatrix {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a p : R) : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) R :=
  !![0, -p; 1, a]

@[simp] lemma frobMatrix_trace {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a p : R) :
    Matrix.trace (frobMatrix a p) = a := by simp [frobMatrix, Matrix.trace_fin_two]

@[simp] lemma frobMatrix_det {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a p : R) :
    Matrix.det (frobMatrix a p) = p := by simp [frobMatrix, Matrix.det_fin_two]

/-- Eichler–Shimura for the Frobenius companion matrix: `Frob² = a·Frob − p·1`. -/
theorem frobMatrix_eichlerShimura {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a p : R) :
    (frobMatrix a p) * (frobMatrix a p)
      = a • frobMatrix a p - p • (1 : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) R) := by
  have h := eichlerShimura (frobMatrix a p)
  rwa [frobMatrix_trace, frobMatrix_det] at h

end EichlerShimuraGL2

# Computational Evidence — Sharpness of the approximate Carathéodory `R/√k` rate

Configuration under test: an orthonormal frame `e₁,…,eₙ` in `ℝⁿ` (so `R = 1`),
target point `x = (1/n) Σ eᵢ` (the centroid). For a selection `f : Fin k → Fin n`
the candidate is the `k`-term average `y = (1/k) Σⱼ e(f j)`. We track the squared
error `‖x − y‖²`.

The formal results are:
- upper bound (`maurey_sqrt`, `R = 1`): `∃ f, ‖x − y‖² ≤ 1/k`;
- lower bound (`sharp_lower_bound`): `∀ f, ‖x − y‖² ≥ 1/k − 1/n`;
- exact optimum for `k ≤ n` (`sharp_optimum`): `min_f ‖x − y‖² = 1/k − 1/n`,
  attained by any `k` **distinct** indices.

## 1. Small-case calculations (best `k`-term error, distinct indices)

With distinct indices the error is `‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − 2⟪x,y⟫ = 1/n + 1/k − 2/n
= 1/k − 1/n`. Direct coordinate checks:

| n | k | choose f      | x                | y                 | ‖x−y‖²        | 1/k − 1/n |
|---|---|---------------|------------------|-------------------|---------------|-----------|
| 3 | 1 | {1}           | (⅓,⅓,⅓)          | (1,0,0)           | 4/9+1/9+1/9=⅔ | 1 − ⅓ = ⅔ |
| 3 | 2 | {1,2}         | (⅓,⅓,⅓)          | (½,½,0)           | 1/36+1/36+1/9=⅙ | ½ − ⅓ = ⅙ |
| 3 | 3 | {1,2,3}       | (⅓,⅓,⅓)          | (⅓,⅓,⅓)           | 0             | ⅓ − ⅓ = 0 |
| 4 | 2 | {1,2}         | (¼,¼,¼,¼)        | (½,½,0,0)         | 2·(¼)²+2·(¼)²=¼ | ½ − ¼ = ¼ |

All four rows confirm `min error = 1/k − 1/n` exactly.

## 2. Collision-count engine (why the lower bound is `1/k`, not `0`)

`‖x − y‖² = (1/k²)·C − 1/n` where `C = Σⱼ Σₗ [f j = f l]` is the number of
ordered collisions of the multiset `f`. The `k` diagonal pairs give `C ≥ k`
always, hence `‖x − y‖² ≥ 1/k − 1/n`. Repetition only *raises* `C`:

| f (n=3,k=3)   | collisions C | (1/9)C | error = (1/9)C − 1/3 |
|---------------|--------------|--------|----------------------|
| {1,2,3}       | 3            | 1/3    | 0       (optimal)    |
| {1,1,2}       | 5            | 5/9    | 2/9                  |
| {1,1,1}       | 9            | 1      | 2/3                  |

So a "lazy" selection that reuses indices is strictly worse — the optimum needs
distinct indices, matching `sharp_optimum`'s `k ≤ n` hypothesis.

## 3. Window width is dimension-only

The two-sided window is `[1/k − 1/n, 1/k]`, width `1/n`, **independent of `k`**:

| n   | width 1/n |
|-----|-----------|
| 2   | 0.5       |
| 10  | 0.1       |
| 100 | 0.01      |
| →∞  | → 0       |

As `n → ∞` the optimum `→ 1/k`, so Maurey's `1/k` upper bound (`R = 1`) is
asymptotically exact: the `k`-dependence cannot be improved.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

We searched for a selection beating `1/k − 1/n` (which would refute
`sharp_lower_bound`). None exists: any `f` has `C ≥ k`, forcing
`‖x − y‖² ≥ 1/k − 1/n`. The bound is met with equality by every injective `f`.
No counterexample found; the inequality is tight.

(All numeric rows above are exact rationals computed by hand from orthonormal
coordinates; the formal Lean proofs in `Sharpness.lean` / `SharpBridge.lean`
discharge the general statements with zero `sorry`s.)

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Sharp approximate Carathéodory & iterated Delaunay refinement

Derived from this cycle's findings (`Maurey.lean`, `MaureyGeneral.lean`,
`Contraction.lean`, `Bridge.lean`, and the new `Sharpness.lean` / `SharpBridge.lean`).
This cycle established a **two-sided** law for the best `k`-term Carathéodory error
of the orthonormal centroid frame: it lies in `[1/k − 1/n, 1/k]`, and equals
exactly `1/k − 1/n` for `k ≤ n`. The looseness is governed by the **dimension**
`n`, not the sample size `k`. The conjectures below push on that structural fact.

## D1. The window width is *always* the centroid's own norm

**Conjecture.** For any finite family `V₁,…,Vₘ` of unit vectors with centroid
`x = (1/m) Σ Vᵢ`, the optimal `k`-term (with-repetition) squared error satisfies
`min_f ‖x − (1/k) Σ V(f j)‖² ∈ [ (1/k)·(1 − ‖x‖²·k? ) , 1/k ]`, with the *additive*
gap to `1/k` equal to exactly `‖x‖²` whenever the family is "balanced" (its Gram
matrix has constant row sums), generalizing the `1/n = ‖centroid‖²` identity.

The key insight is that in `sq_dist_eq` the only slack term is `−‖x‖²`, so the
gap between the Maurey upper bound and the true optimum is *intrinsic to `x`*, not
to the sampling — the orthonormal case (`‖x‖² = 1/n`) is just the cleanest witness.

Why now? `sq_dist_eq` already isolates `‖x − y‖² = (1/k²)·(collision Gram) − ‖x‖²`
for arbitrary frames; only the collision lower bound `≥ k` used orthonormality, so
the conjecture is one Gram-matrix estimate away from the proved skeleton.

## D2. Sharpness across `ℓ_p`: the exponent `1 − 1/p` is two-sided

**Conjecture.** In `ℓ_p^n` (`2 ≤ p < ∞`) the centroid-of-basis configuration forces
`min_f ‖x − y‖_p^? ≥ c_p · k^{-(1 − 1/p)}` for a constant `c_p > 0`, matching the
known Maurey/Barman upper bound `O(k^{-(1−1/p)})` — i.e. the empirical-method
exponent is sharp for every `p ≥ 2`, not just `p = 2`.

The key insight is that the `p = 2` collision-count argument (`[f j = f l] ≥
[j = l]`) is an instance of a general "self-overlap ≥ multiplicity" bound that
survives in `ℓ_p` after replacing inner products by the `p`-th power pairing.

Why now? Our `ℓ_2` proof needs only one inequality on top of identities; the
`ℓ_p` version isolates exactly which step must be replaced (the Gram collapse),
making it a concrete, falsifiable target rather than a vague generalization.

## D3. Minicenter Delaunay refinement has a *sharp* contraction constant

**Conjecture.** For `d`-simplex minicenter (smallest-enclosing-ball center)
refinement, the per-step diameter contraction factor `λ_d` is bounded *and* the
bound is attained: `λ_d = √(2(d+1)/d)` for the regular simplex, with the segment
case `λ_1 = 2` of `Contraction.lean` as the `d = 1` instance.

The key insight is that the segment base case (`minicenter_segment_halves`,
`λ = 2`) is the `d = 1` value of a single closed-form `λ_d`, because the
minicenter of a regular `d`-simplex splits each edge in a ratio fixed by the
circumradius-to-edge formula.

Why now? `Contraction.lean` already packages contraction as a reusable
`ContractionProcess` and proves the `d = 1` constant *geometrically*; supplying
`λ_d` for higher `d` slots directly into `diam_le_pow` with no new metric
machinery.

## D4. The refinement budget is sharp, not just finite

**Conjecture.** The cumulative covering bound `∑ cov k ≤ D·λ/(λ−1)` of
`Bridge.lean` is tight: there is a refinement trajectory (the regular-simplex
bisection of `Contraction.lean`) whose total covering error equals
`D·λ/(λ−1)` up to a factor `1 + o(1)`, so no per-step contraction analysis can
promise a smaller cumulative budget.

The key insight is that the geometric series bounding the budget is saturated
exactly when each step contracts by *precisely* `1/λ` (equality in `contracts`),
which the segment bisection achieves (`segmentBisection`, equality form).

Why now? `Bridge.total_budget` gives the closed-form upper bound and
`segmentBisection` already realizes equality per step; matching the *sum* is a
geometric-series equality check, directly testable.

## D5. A two-sided coreset law for approximate Carathéodory

**Conjecture.** Combining D1 and the upper bound, the *expected* squared error of
the empirical method equals the optimum up to a factor `2`: for the centroid
frame, `E_f ‖x − y‖² = 1/k − 1/n` is *exactly* the random-selection mean (not just
an upper bound), so the probabilistic method is, in expectation, optimal — there
is no gap between "best" and "average" `k`-term selection on balanced frames.

The key insight is that `expectation_bound` (in `MaureyGeneral.lean`) computes the
mean error as `τ/k` with `τ = Σ pᵢ‖x − Vᵢ‖²`, and for the orthonormal centroid
`τ = 1 − 1/n`, giving mean `= (1 − 1/n)/k`, while the optimum is `1/k − 1/n`;
these differ by `(1/n)(1 − 1/k)`, an explicitly bounded, dimension-only gap.

Why now? Both quantities are already formalized (`expectation_bound` and
`sharp_optimum`); their difference is a one-line algebraic identity, so the
"mean = optimum up to dimension" statement is immediately checkable and would
quantify exactly how lossless Maurey's averaging is.

# Computational Evidence — Erdős–Rényi threshold phenomena

All quantities below are the *exact* first-moment expectations proved in
`Concrete.lean` (`E[#triangles] = C(n,3)·p³`, `E[#isolated] = n·(1−p)^{n−1}`),
evaluated numerically to locate the thresholds before the formal limit proofs.

## 1. Triangle critical window, `p = c/n` (here `c = 1`)

Conjecture: `C(n,3)·(c/n)³ → c³/6`. For `c = 1` the target is `1/6 ≈ 0.166667`.

| n      | E[#triangles] = C(n,3)·(1/n)³ |
|--------|-------------------------------|
| 10     | 0.120000 |
| 50     | 0.156800 |
| 100    | 0.161700 |
| 1000   | 0.166167 |
| 10000  | 0.166617 |

Monotone convergence to `1/6`. This pins the triangle threshold at `p = 1/n`:
below it (`n·p → 0`) the mean → 0, above it (`n·p → ∞`) the mean → ∞.
→ formalized as `tendsto_expected_triangles`, `subcritical_triangles_vanish`,
`supercritical_triangles_blowup`.

## 2. Isolated vertices at the giant-component scale `p = c/n` (here `c = 1`)

Conjecture: `n·(1−c/n)^{n−1} → ∞`, with the per-vertex factor `(1−c/n)^{n−1} → e^{−c}`.
For `c = 1`, `e^{−1} ≈ 0.367879`.

| n      | E[#isolated] | factor (1−1/n)^{n−1} |
|--------|--------------|----------------------|
| 10     | 3.8742   | 0.387420 |
| 50     | 18.5801  | 0.371602 |
| 100    | 36.9730  | 0.369730 |
| 1000   | 368.0635 | 0.368063 |
| 10000  | 3678.9784| 0.367898 |

The factor converges to `1/e`; multiplied by `n → ∞` the expected isolated-vertex
count diverges. So at the scale `p = 1/n` the graph is full of isolated vertices —
the giant-component scale is **strictly below** the connectivity scale.
→ formalized as `isolated_blowup_below_connectivity`.

## 3. Connectivity scale `p = ln n / n` (boundary check)

At the conjectured *connectivity* threshold `p = ln n / n`, the expected number of
isolated vertices should stay of constant order (`n^{1/n} → 1`), not blow up:

| n       | E[#isolated] = n·(1 − ln n/n)^{n−1} |
|---------|-------------------------------------|
| 10      | 0.9486 |
| 100     | 0.9396 |
| 1000    | 0.9831 |
| 100000  | 0.9995 |

The count hovers near `1` (→ 1 as `n → ∞`), consistent with `ln n / n` being the
sharp connectivity threshold (isolated vertices, the last obstruction to
connectivity, are Poisson(1) at the threshold). The sharp two-sided connectivity
statement is left to `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`; the divergence strictly below it
(`p = c/n`) is the formalized result.

## Notes
- No new OEIS sequence arises; the relevant constants are `1/6` (= `C(n,3)/n³`
  limit) and `e^{−c}` (Poisson means).
- No counterexample found: every sampled value matches the predicted limit.

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Erdős–Rényi threshold phenomena

Derived from this cycle's findings in `Model.lean`, `SecondMoment.lean`,
`Concrete.lean`, and the new `Threshold.lean`. This cycle established the
*moment-method skeleton* (first moment `firstMoment`, second moment
`second_moment_zero`, exact expectations `expected_triangles`,

`supercritical_triangles_blowup`, `isolated_blowup_below_connectivity`). The
following conjectures push toward the *sharp two-sided* thresholds.

## 1. Supercritical triangle appearance via the second moment method
**Conjecture.** If `n·pₙ → ∞` and `pₙ ≤ 1`, then `G(n, pₙ)` contains a triangle
with high probability: `ℙ(#triangles = 0) → 0`.
*The key insight is* that `second_moment_zero` reduces this to showing
`Var(#triangles)/E[#triangles]² → 0`, and the variance splits over pairs of
triangles by their shared-edge count (0, 1, or shared edge ⇒ shared vertex),
each contribution computable by the same `prob_allPresent` independence identity
already proved in `Model.lean`.
*Why now?* The exact first moment (`expected_triangles`) and the abstract second
moment bound (`second_moment_zero`) are both formalized; only the variance
decomposition lemma is missing, and it is a finite `Finset` computation of the
type this cycle already automated.

## 2. Sharp connectivity threshold at `p = ln n / n`
**Conjecture.** For `pₙ = (ln n + cₙ)/n`: if `cₙ → +∞` then `G(n, pₙ)` is
connected whp, and if `cₙ → −∞` then it is disconnected whp; at `cₙ → c` the
number of isolated vertices is asymptotically `Poisson(e^{−c})`.
*The key insight is* that isolated vertices are the dominant obstruction: the
exact expectation `n·(1−p)^{n−1}` (this cycle, `expected_isolated`) tends to
`e^{−c}`, and a second-moment computation shows the isolated-vertex count is
concentrated, so connectivity is governed entirely by whether that mean → 0.
*Why now?* `isolated_blowup_below_connectivity` already proves the divergence
strictly below the threshold; extending the limit computation from `p = c/n` to
`p = (ln n + c)/n` needs only the `(1 + x/n)^n → eˣ` machinery
(`Real.tendsto_one_add_div_pow_exp`) already used here.

## 3. General subgraph threshold at the balanced density `p = n^{−1/m(H)}`
**Conjecture.** For a fixed graph `H` with maximum edge-density
`m(H) = max_{H'⊆H} e(H')/v(H')`, the threshold for containing a copy of `H` is
`p = n^{−1/m(H)}`: below it `H` is absent whp, above it present whp.
*The key insight is* that `expectation_subgraphCount` already gives the first
moment `(#copies)·p^{e(H)}`, and the densest subgraph `H'` controls the second
moment, so the threshold is exactly where the *balanced* expected count is `Θ(1)`.
*Why now?* `expectation_subgraphCount_uniform` formalizes the uniform first moment
for arbitrary edge-set families; the triangle case (`m = 3/3 = 1`, threshold
`1/n`) is now fully proved and is the `H = K₃` instance of this statement.

## 4. Giant-component phase transition at `p = c/n`
**Conjecture.** For `pₙ = c/n`: if `c < 1` the largest component has size
`O(log n)` whp, while if `c > 1` there is a unique component of size `Θ(n)` whp.
*The key insight is* that the local neighborhood exploration of `G(n, c/n)` is
approximated by a Galton–Watson branching process with mean offspring `c`, whose
survival probability is positive iff `c > 1`; the triangle-count constant `c³/6`
proved here is the first nontrivial moment of that limiting local structure.
*Why now?* `tendsto_ER_expected_triangles` confirms the `c/n` scale produces a
nondegenerate `Θ(1)` count of small cycles — the exact regime where the
branching-process heuristic becomes sharp.

## 5. Poisson limit for triangle counts in the critical window
**Conjecture.** At `p = c/n`, the number of triangles converges in distribution
to `Poisson(c³/6)`.
*The key insight is* that the factorial moments of the triangle count converge to
the powers of `c³/6` (the method of moments), and each factorial moment is a
first-moment computation over ordered tuples of triangles of exactly the form
`expectation_subgraphCount` handles.
*Why now?* The mean `c³/6` is now proved (`tendsto_expected_triangles`); the
method of moments needs only higher factorial moments, which are the same
`prob_allPresent` product identities iterated.
